newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Religious battle of the sexes at Jewish shrine.
newsitem.headline: Religious battle of the sexes at Jewish shrine.

text.p: Men shouted in anger and hurled a folding chair at a group of 60 Jewish women worshippers who challenged traditional ultra-Orthodox control of prayers at Jerusalem's Wailing Wall on Tuesday.

An Israel Radio reporter at the Wall said the ultra-Orthodox men, though separated from the women by a divider, objected to the women wearing religious skullcaps and prayer shawls which according to Orthodox ritual are supposed to be worn by men.
"This is another effort to return us to the Middle Ages," complained Anat Maor, a woman and a leftist member of parliament.
"Just as men have pluralism and an interpretation of religion, so should women have the right to wear skullcaps," she told the radio.

No one was hurt in the incident. Police moved the women to an area some 60 metres (yards) away where, under police protection, they continued their prayers marking the start of the Jewish month of Kislev.

The Wall is the sole remnant of the retaining wall around the ancient Jewish Temple, and the battle was the latest in a religious war going back years at the holy site. The women also seek to read from the Torah scroll.

Secular Israelis complain that Orthodox Jews, backed by religious political parties crucial to Israeli coalition governments, have an exclusive grip on religious services in the Jewish state such as marriages, divorces and burials.

Women who pray at the Wall are expected to cover their arms and legs in accordance with Orthodox tradition. They are not supposed to read from the Torah and must keep their voices low so as not to disturb the men across the way.
Religious officials said the women should have known better.

"Everyone knows the Wall is a holy place. This is a place where for 2,000 years the public has gone to pray. Everyone knows this issue could cause big disturbances," said Avi Bluestein, director-general of the religious affairs ministry.
He said a committee to study the issue would make its recommendations in four months.

In 1994 Israel's High Court of Justice recommended the government, which administers the Wall, set up the committee to see if women could be allowed to carry out the rituals without offending other worshippers.
